summary.text: Since \(28749=3\cdot7\cdot37\cdot37\) and \(373737=13\cdot28749\), the target is composite and its concatenation is divisible by it. An exhaustive trial-division computation for every smaller integer shows that either its prime-factor list has length at most one or its concatenation has positive residue; every composite greater than one has at least two prime factors, so no smaller composite has residue zero.

full_proof.text:
Let the prime factors of an integer \(n\ge 2\), written with multiplicity and in nondecreasing order, be
\[
 p_1\le p_2\le\cdots\le p_r.
\]
If \(\ell(x)\) denotes the number of decimal digits of the positive integer \(x\), define the decimal concatenation recursively by
\[
 C_0=0,\qquad C_j=C_{j-1}10^{\ell(p_j)}+p_j\quad(1\le j\le r).
\]
Thus \(C_r\) is the integer whose decimal representation is obtained by writing \(p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_r\) successively. The sequence in the question is
\[
 a(n)=C_r\bmod n
\]
for \(n\ge2\) (and may be set equal to \(0\) for \(n<2\)). We prove that \(28749\) is composite, that \(a(28749)=0\), and that no smaller composite integer has remainder zero.

The proof of the last assertion is a finite exhaustive calculation. To make that calculation mathematically explicit and to justify that it computes precisely the required quantity, we first describe the factorization, digit-counting, and range-checking procedures used in it.

### 1. Correctness of the trial-division factorization

For nonnegative integers \(f,n,d\), define a list \(F(f,n,d)\) by the following recursion:

1. If \(f=0\), return the empty list.
2. If \(f>0\) and \(n<2\), return the empty list.
3. Otherwise, if \(d\mid n\), put \(d\) at the front of \(F(f-1,n/d,d)\).
4. If \(d\nmid n\) and \(d^2>n\), return the one-element list \([n]\).
5. In the remaining case, return \(F(f-1,n,d+1)\).

For the finite computation below, the factor list assigned to \(n\) is
\[
 \operatorname{Fact}(n)=F(2n,n,2).
\]
We now prove that this is exactly the nondecreasing prime-factor list of \(n\).

The relevant invariant for a call \(F(f,n,d)\) is:
\[
 d\ge2,\quad n\ge1,\quad\text{and every divisor }m\mid n\text{ with }m\ge2\text{ satisfies }m\ge d.
\]
In other words, trial division has already ruled out every possible divisor from \(2\) through \(d-1\). Under this invariant and with sufficient remaining recursion, the returned list has the following four properties:

* its product is \(n\);
* every entry is prime;
* its entries are nondecreasing;
* every entry is at least \(d\).

Here is the induction proving these claims. If \(n<2\), the condition \(n\ge1\) forces \(n=1\), and the empty list has product \(1\), so all four assertions hold.

Suppose next that \(d\mid n\). Since no divisor of \(n\) that is at least \(2\) is smaller than \(d\), the number \(d\) is prime. Indeed, if \(d\) had a proper divisor \(m\) with \(1<m<d\), then \(m\mid d\mid n\), contradicting the invariant. Apply the recursion to \(n/d\) with the same candidate divisor \(d\). Every divisor \(m\ge2\) of \(n/d\) is also a divisor of \(n\), so it is at least \(d\); hence the invariant persists. By induction the recursive list consists of primes at least \(d\), is sorted, and has product \(n/d\). Prefixing \(d\) therefore leaves the list sorted and prime and gives product
\[
 d(n/d)=n.
\]

Suppose that \(d\nmid n\) and \(d^2>n\). Then \(n\) is prime. For if \(n=uv\) were a nontrivial factorization, with \(u,v\ge2\), both \(u\) and \(v\) would be divisors of \(n\). The invariant would imply \(u,v\ge d\), whence \(n=uv\ge d^2\), contrary to \(d^2>n\). Thus returning \([n]\) has all the claimed properties.

Finally, suppose \(d\nmid n\) and \(d^2\le n\). The recursion advances from \(d\) to \(d+1\). The old invariant already excludes divisors below \(d\), and the test \(d\nmid n\) excludes \(d\) itself. Consequently every divisor of \(n\) that is at least \(2\) is at least \(d+1\), exactly the invariant needed for the next call. The induction then applies unchanged.

There is enough recursion in the initial call \(F(2n,n,2)\). One convenient quantitative bound is that a call satisfying the invariant needs no more than
\[
 2n+2-d
\]
steps. If a factor \(d\) is removed, then \(d\ge2\), so \(2(n/d)\le n\), and the required bound strictly decreases within the remaining allowance. If no factor is removed and \(d\) is increased by one, the bound decreases by one. Thus the recursion cannot run out before one of the terminal cases is reached.

It follows that for every positive \(n\), \(\operatorname{Fact}(n)\) is a nondecreasing list of primes whose product is \(n\). The multiset of prime factors of a positive integer is unique, so this list is precisely the usual prime-factor list, including multiplicities. The same conclusion is immediate for \(n=0\) under the adopted empty-list convention, although only positive integers matter in the composite case.

### 2. Correctness of decimal concatenation

The finite calculation counts decimal digits by the recurrence
\[
 D(0)=0,
 \qquad
 D(k)=1+D(\lfloor k/10\rfloor)\quad(k>0).
\]
Equivalently, one can give this recurrence a finite counter larger than \(k\); division by \(10\) strictly decreases every positive argument, so the counter never expires. We verify by induction that \(D(k)\) is the length of the base-10 digit list of \(k\). This is immediate for \(k=0\). For \(k>0\), the last decimal digit contributes one digit and the remaining digits are exactly those of \(\lfloor k/10\rfloor\), so
\[
 \ell(k)=1+\ell(\lfloor k/10\rfloor)=1+D(\lfloor k/10\rfloor)=D(k).
\]

Starting with accumulator \(0\), the calculation processes the entries \(q\) of \(\operatorname{Fact}(n)\) from left to right and replaces an accumulator \(x\) by
\[
 x10^{D(q)}+q.
\]
Since \(D(q)=\ell(q)\) and \(\operatorname{Fact}(n)\) is the ordered prime-factor list, this operation produces exactly the concatenated integer \(C_r\). Reducing the final accumulator modulo \(n\) therefore gives exactly \(a(n)\). Denote this directly computed remainder by \(a_*(n)\); we have established
\[
 a_*(n)=a(n)
\]
for every \(n\).

### 3. The finite exclusion calculation

For each nonnegative integer \(m\), consider the Boolean assertion
\[
 P(m):\quad
 \bigl(|\operatorname{Fact}(m)|\le1\bigr)
 \ \text{or}\ 
 \bigl(1\le a_*(m)\bigr).
\]
Because \(a_*(m)\) is a nonnegative remainder, its second alternative is simply the assertion that the remainder is nonzero.

The exhaustive integer calculation, using exactly the trial-division and concatenation recurrences above, gives
\[
 P(m)\quad\text{for every }0\le m<28749.
\]
For completeness, the range was divided into the following disjoint blocks. For each \(j=0,1,\ldots,27\), all one thousand values in
\[
 1000j\le m<1000(j+1)
\]
were checked, and all 749 values in
\[
 28000\le m<28749
\]
were checked. Every block returned true.

One can describe the exact exhaustive range evaluation without hiding any sampling assumption. Given a predicate \(P\), a starting point \(L\), a length \(s\), and a nonnegative depth \(t\), define \(R(P,t,L,s)\) as follows. For \(s=0\), it is true; for \(s=1\), it is \(P(L)\). For \(s\ge2\), put \(u=\lfloor s/2\rfloor\) and set
\[
 R(P,t,L,s)=R(P,t-1,L,u)\wedge
 R(P,t-1,L+u,s-u).
\]
At depth zero, the only cases used are lengths zero or one. By induction on \(t\), whenever \(s\le2^t\), the equality \(R(P,t,L,s)=\mathrm{true}\) implies
\[
 P(i)=\mathrm{true}\qquad(L\le i<L+s).
\]
Indeed, for a range of length at least two, an index \(i\) lies either in the left half \([L,L+u)\) or in the right half \([L+u,L+s)\), and the corresponding induction hypothesis applies. Since \(1000\le2^{10}=1024\) and \(749\le1024\), depth ten suffices for every block above. Exact evaluation of this recurrence gave
\[
 R(P,10,1000j,1000)=\mathrm{true}\quad(0\le j\le27)
\]
and
\[
 R(P,10,28000,749)=\mathrm{true}.
\]
Thus the asserted universal statement \(P(m)\) for \(m<28749\) follows from the range-recursion induction. The role of this finite calculation is specifically to establish, for every integer below the proposed first example, the dichotomy “at most one prime factor, or nonzero concatenation remainder.”

We next explain why that dichotomy rules out every smaller composite. If \(n>1\) is composite, its prime-factor list has length at least two. It cannot be empty because its entries must have product \(n>1\). If it had exactly one entry \(p\), then the product identity would give \(n=p\); since every entry of the factor list is prime, \(n\) itself would be prime, contrary to compositeness. Therefore
\[
 |
 \operatorname{Fact}(n)|\ge2
\]
for every composite \(n\).

Now let \(n<28749\) be composite. The exhaustive result says that \(P(n)\) holds. Its first alternative, \(|\operatorname{Fact}(n)|\le1\), contradicts the preceding inequality. Hence its second alternative must hold:
\[
 1\le a_*(n).
\]
Since \(a_*(n)=a(n)\), this gives \(a(n)\ne0\). Thus no composite integer below \(28749\) has a zero term.

### 4. The value at \(28749\)

Finally,
\[
 28749=3\cdot7\cdot37\cdot37.
\]
The factors \(3,7,37,37\) are prime and nondecreasing, so they are the prime factors with multiplicity in the required order. In particular, \(28749=3\cdot9583\) with both factors greater than one, so \(28749\) is composite.

Concatenating those factors gives
\[
 3\,\Vert\,7\,\Vert\,37\,\Vert\,37=373737.
\]
A direct multiplication shows
\[
 373737=13\cdot28749.
\]
Consequently
\[
 a(28749)=373737\bmod28749=0.
\]

We have shown both that \(28749\) is a composite index with \(a(28749)=0\), and that every smaller composite index has a nonzero remainder. Therefore the first composite number \(n\) for which \(a(n)=0\) is \(28749\).
